profile.behavior: Usually solitary; walks slowly through shallow freshwater, bobbing its rear and sometimes trembling a foot to stir prey. Picks prey by sight, probes only occasionally, and may briefly hold its wings raised after landing.
field_marks: Dark olive-brown upperparts neatly spotted with white
Finely streaked gray-brown head, neck, and upper breast above a white belly
Long folded wings and a short, dark-centered tail with pale barred outer feathers
profile.habitat: Quiet freshwater wetlands, especially wooded ponds, stream edges, swamps, bogs, muddy pools, ditches, and flooded fields; generally avoids tidal flats and salt marshes.

findings: The primary specimen is a convincing Solitary Sandpiper: dark olive-brown, white-spotted upperparts; finely streaked head, neck, and upper breast; clean white belly; bold complete white eye-ring; thin straight dark bill; olive-yellow legs; long folded wings; and a dark-centered, pale-barred tail all agree with the reference photos and live identification sources.

Overall proportions are credible, though the legs and neck are slightly elongated relative to several attached photographs; the difference remains within an acceptable field-illustration range and does not suggest another species.
The primary specimen has one head, one bill, two overlapping folded wings, two anatomically coherent legs and feet, and one tail. No duplicated or extraneous anatomy is attached.

The detached spread-wing and head studies are clearly supplementary. Both are anatomically coherent and reproduce the species’ pointed wing, spotted upperwing, eye-ring, streaked face, and thin straight bill consistently with the primary specimen.
All visible identification, habitat, and behavior text is legible and matches the proposed wording without duplicated, omitted, substituted, misspelled, or nonsensical words.

The common name, scientific name, and family are correct. All About Birds, Birds of the World, and Animal Diversity Web identify the species as Solitary Sandpiper, Tringa solitaria, family Scolopacidae.

The printed 19–23 cm length, 31–65 g weight, and 55–57 cm wingspan match the current All About Birds identification page. Animal Diversity Web independently supports the 19–23 cm and 31–65 g ranges. Audubon publishes narrower alternative measurements, so the sources are not unanimous, but the plate’s values are directly supported by the cited Cornell source.

The ruler is internally consistent: 19 cm is at the bottom, 23 cm at the top, values increase upward, four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks create five proportional segments, endpoint conversions match the printed range, and the repeated body-length label agrees. “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE” clearly prevents interpreting the printed bird as life-size.
The palette labels and swatches are appropriate to the illustrated plumage and bare-part colors.
